newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sources claim terror link to N.Y. plot.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sources claim terror link to N.Y. plot.

text.p: Law enforcement sources on Friday linked suspects in an alleged New York subway suicide bombing plot to a radical Palestinian group and officials said disaster was only hours away when police seized five bombs.
Two of three men arrested in a raid in New York on Thursday were charged late Friday in their hospital beds where they are recovering from gunshot wounds.

A federal judge presided over the arraignment in a New York hospital, in which 23-year-old Gazi Ibrahim Abu Mezer and 22-year-old Lafi Khalil were charged with conspiracy to blow up a subway and possession of explosives, NBC Television reported.

Earlier, New York Mayor Rudolph Giuliani and Police Commissioner Howard Safir fumed over indications that one of the men, Abu Mezer, had filled out a U.S. immigration application in which he stated that he had been arrested previously in Israel "and accused of being a member of a known terrorist organisation."
"I think it is appropriate to question why this person was allowed into the country announcing that he was part of a terrorist group in Israel," the mayor said.
But Fred Krug, a spokesman for the U.S. State Department's bureau of diplomatic security said, "I would suggest to you that he wouldn't have gotten the visa if he had said that on the application."

Officials told a news conference that a major explosion was prevented when police raided a ramshackle Brooklyn apartment at dawn on Thursday, seizing five potentially deadly pipe bombs and arresting three Middle Eastern men, two of whom were shot and wounded.
The FBI and the New York City police alleged in a joint statement that the suspects intended to target "U.S. and Jewish interests worldwide."
ABC News reported on Friday that Abu Mezer left a note in which he stated his hatred for the United States and for the Jewish poeple.

Quoting unidentified sources, the network said the FBI had found a crudely written suicide note by Abu Mezer that also denounced the persecution of Arabs and expressed his support for the militant Palestinian group, Hamas.

Law enforcement sources said investigators had evidence that the suspects made telephone calls to the Hamas organisation from stores near the apartment in the residential Park Slope neighbourhood of Brooklyn.

"The suspects were using the telephones at the laundromat and grocery store near the apartment where they were staying and we were able to trace the numbers back to Hamas," one law enforcement source told Reuters.

The head of the FBI in New York, James Kallstrom, declined to comment on any possible links between the suspects and the Palestinian Islamic resistance movement Hamas, the group that has claimed responsibility for suicide bombings in Israel.
The latest attack killed 15 people, including two suicide bombers, in a Jerusalem market on Wednesday.

"We have a lot of leads, a lot of things we are going to be looking at," Kallstrom told reporters. "We know a lot about known terrorist groups and we know a lot about people and we know a lot about people we think we should know a lot about."
ABC News said Abu Mezer told the FBI that he had bought materials to make the bombs during a recent trip to Greenville, N.C and said that was where he met Khalil.

A New York attorney for Moussa Abu Marzook, leader of the political wing of Hamas, said that his client called the suspects "cowboys" who were probably upset by the conditions of the Palestinian people.

"It's absolutely absurd," Stanley Cohen quoted Marzook as saying from Jordan, where he was deported in May after being held without trial for two years in a U.S. prison. "It's ridiculous and a total lie that Hamas had anything to do with these guys wanting to plant pipe bombs."

A day after the raid, security was tightened around New York subways, trains, buses, courthouses and houses of worship. The security concerns were reminiscent of the aftermath of the February 1993 bombing of the World Trade Centre by Moslem militants in which six people were killed and more than 1,000 injured.
"I think we were close to a disaster here, but it didn't happen. And that's the good news," Kallstrom said. "Whether it was 12 hours or 18 hours, 24 or 36 is irrelevant."

Police stormed the apartment on a tipoff from a man who lived in the building, police sources said. Officers opened fire on the suspects after one of them lunged at one of the pipe bombs in an attempt to activate it, officials said.
"The police officers, by acting as quickly as they did, probably prevented a pretty bad explosion right in that neighbourhood," Giuliani said.
In Washington, President Bill Clinton praised police but said it was too early to draw conclusions about the case.

A federal complaint filed Thursday named Abu Mezer and 22-year-old Lafi Khalil as two of the suspects being held on criminal charges. A third suspect, not named by authorities, was being held as allegedly being in the United States illegally, officials said.
